newsitem.title: GERMANY: German economy minister presses Ukraine to reform.
newsitem.headline: German economy minister presses Ukraine to reform.

text.p: German Economy Minister Guenter Rexrodt on Tuesday urged Ukraine to push ahead with its economic reforms if it hoped to attract badly-needed foreign investment.
"Every week, every month is becoming more urgent and a system of reforms is important," Rexrodt, speaking through an interpreter, told a conference on investment in Ukraine.
"Interest in Ukraine is enormous but you have to create conditions for foreign investors to go to Ukraine," he said.
"There are legal inconsistencies, red tape and a disproportionate demand for administrative fees and royalties," Rexrodt added.

Foreign investors have cited inconsistent and changing laws, a punitive tax system and demands for bribes as the main reasons the former Soviet republic has attracted only about $1.5 billion from abroad since independence in 1991.

Ukraine's parliament, which approved the 1997 budget late last week, is expected to approve a series of tax reform measures by the end of the year and the government plans to streamline the number of licenses required to start a business.
Rexrodt also urged Ukraine to meet reform measures demanded by international funding bodies such as the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
IMF officials said last week Ukraine may receive an interim stand-by credit until it meets 41 conditions to qualify for a three-year, $2.5 to $3 billion Extended Fund Facility.
Rexrodt said Ukraine should fulfil an agreement with the Group of Seven (G7) wealthy industrial nations to close the Chernobyl nuclear power plant by 2000.
But Ukraine, which promised the G7 last year to shut the notorious nuclear plant by 2000 in exchange for $3.1 billion, expressed disappointment after last month's Denver summit.

At the summit, the G7 offered $300 million instead of the $780 million Ukraine wanted to rebuild the structure enclosing the ruined reactor, site of what was arguably the world's worst peace-time nuclear accident.
